P/B compares the market value of the shares with the accounting book value of net assets. It is often used for early stage or pre revenue biotechs where earnings are still negative. data.title: Valero Energy Corporation (NYSE:VLO) Looks Like A Good Stock, And It's Going Ex-Dividend Soon
data.description:
Readers hoping to buy Valero Energy Corporation (NYSE:VLO) for its dividend will need to make their move shortly, as the stock is about to trade ex-dividend. Typically, the ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade takes at least one business day to settle. In other words, investors can purchase Valero Energy's shares before the 24th of November in order to be eligible for the dividend, which will be paid on the 21st of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$1.20 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$4.80 to shareholders. Looking at the last 12 months of distributions, Valero Energy has a trailing yield of approximately 1.4% on its current stock price of US$343.70. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. That's why we should always check whether the dividend payments appear sustainable, and if the company is growing.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

If a company pays out more in dividends than it earned, then the dividend might become unsustainable - hardly an ideal situation. Valero Energy has a low and conservative payout ratio of just 11% of its income after tax. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. The good news is it paid out just 9.3% of its free cash flow in the last year.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Companies with consistently growing earnings per share generally make the best dividend stocks, as they usually find it easier to grow dividends per share. If earnings fall far enough, the company could be forced to cut its dividend. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at Valero Energy, with earnings per share up 4.8% on average over the last five years. Growth has been anaemic. Yet with more than 75% of its earnings being kept in the business, there is ample room to reinvest in growth or lift the payout ratio - either of which could increase the dividend.

Another key way to measure a company's dividend prospects is by measuring its historical rate of dividend growth. Valero Energy has delivered an average of 7.2% per year annual increase in its dividend, based on the past 10 years of dividend payments. We're glad to see dividends rising alongside earnings over a number of years, which may be a sign the company intends to share the growth with shareholders.

Final Takeaway

Is Valero Energy worth buying for its dividend? Earnings per share growth has been growing somewhat, and Valero Energy is paying out less than half its earnings and cash flow as dividends. This is interesting for a few reasons, as it suggests management may be reinvesting heavily in the business, but it also provides room to increase the dividend in time. We would prefer to see earnings growing faster, but the best dividend stocks over the long term typically combine significant earnings per share growth with a low payout ratio, and Valero Energy is halfway there. data.title: What BT Group Bulls Got Right
data.description:
If you watched BT Group this year, the development that jumped out was not a new fibre contract but a reshaped pension deal that freed room for shareholder distributions. For BT Group shareholders, the return over the past year was 28.2%, including dividends. If you had been weighing a purchase back in November 2025, what belief about pensions, cash generation and future payouts would have justified pressing the buy button before that news landed?

If the move has made BT Group harder to judge, start where the gap is still open and scan 14 high quality undervalued stocks.

The Two Stories BT Group Investors Were Arguing About

BT Group shares cost £1.77 at the start of the period, and investors were effectively choosing between two very different stories about what that price already implied.

The bullish narrative saw fibre build and 5G as the engine, with a Fair Value of £2.1. This was a price those assumptions pointed to if revenue declined 0.9% a year while profit margin reached 8.5% and the future P/E sat at 15.5x.

The bearish script put more weight on fixed line decline and heavy obligations, with a Fair Value of £1.3 and a risk that structural revenue pressure and pension and debt costs would keep squeezing flexibility.

What The Results Changed For The BT Group Debate

The clearest shift came from BT Group’s pension update. The deficit moved to £2.7b with funding at 92.3%, alongside a new agreement that lets the business return up to £1.5b this year and £2b by 2030 without extra pension payments. That directly supported the bullish focus on financial flexibility, while rising H1 2027 net income and a higher 9.5% net margin challenged the most cautious case. The evidence cut both ways.

The whole episode turned on one assumption: you were really assessing whether BT Group could turn pension strain into room for cash returns without weakening operations. When you assess another telecom stock, track pension or long term liabilities alongside net margin in the results, and check how any new funding deal changes the allowable cash that can leave the business.

What BT Group’s Current Price Already Assumes

BT Group now trades at £2.15, and the bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St argues that its Fair Value sits below that level. The Narrative frames revenue pressure and execution risk on the cost programme as the key friction against the recent 28.2% gain over the past year.

A buyer today is effectively assuming BT’s fibre build and cost cuts can offset legacy declines and support solid free cash flow. The Narrative then asks how exposed that belief is if revenue keeps weakening while higher labour and tax costs absorb more of the planned savings.

"The main factor that needs to work in BT Group’s favor is successful delivery of its extended cost transformation and network migration program, so that large planned cost savings and efficiency gains translate into resilient earnings and cash generation. The current valuation suggests the market is already accounting for successful fiber rollout, cash flow growth and ongoing dividend increases, which may leave limited room for disappointment in BT Group’s share price."
